The wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches approximately 1.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 1.2 grams], a modest body mass that underscores the limited resources available in the mesopelagic zone. Comparisons with congeners suggest that this species has converged on a slow-paced lifestyle, with delayed maturation and prolonged reproductive periods being typical of small lanternfishes that inhabit low-productivity waters.

Puberty in Notolychnus valdiviae is attained at a standard length of 1.7 cm [Lp = 1.7 cm], a threshold that is reached relatively early in the growth trajectory. At this size, the wet weight of the individual is roughly 0.02 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.02 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain required to reach the adult body size. The length at puberty corresponds to approximately 27 percent of the ultimate length, a proportion that is consistent with the pattern seen in other myctophids that begin reproducing while still actively growing. This early maturation allows the species to exploit a narrow window of favourable conditions in the oligotrophic waters it inhabits.

This modest initial mass is typical of myctophids that produce oligolecthial eggs with limited per-offspring investment, a trade-off that favours higher fecundity at the expense of individual larval provisioning.

Under the stable thermal conditions of the mesopelagic zone, where ambient temperatures hover near 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the lifespan of Notolychnus valdiviae extends to about 3 years [am = about 3 years]. This longevity is comparable to that of other small myctophids and is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes reproductive persistence over rapid turnover. The annual reproductive output at this same temperature is approximately 106 eggs per female per year [Ri = approximately 106 eggs per female per year], a rate that results from the combination of moderate batch fecundity and intermittent spawning events spread across the year.

The interaction between body size and reproductive output in Notolychnus valdiviae reveals a tightly constrained energetic budget. The modest ultimate wet weight of 1.2 grams [Wwi = 1.2 grams] limits the volume of the body cavity available for developing oocytes, which in turn constrains the batch fecundity that can be accommodated. The age at first reproduction, which likely follows soon after the attainment of puberty at a length of 1.7 cm [Lp = 1.7 cm], allows the species to begin contributing to the next generation while still investing in somatic growth. This pattern of overlapping growth and reproduction is a common feature among small, short-lived mesopelagic teleosts that inhabit thermally stable but food-limited environments.
